processing: Bred for steamed sencha, and also made into pan-fired kamairicha, oolong and black tea, each processed in the usual way for that style.
harvest_season: Spring, slightly after Yabukita, about one to three days later; a second flush also yields well.
appearance_liquor: As sencha, clear pale yellow-green, typical of the style.
appearance_wet: Soft bright-green leaf, typical of sencha.
taste_profile: Known for its aroma, described as milky, floral and refreshing, and clearly different from Yabukita.

brewing.notes: These are sencha settings. For an oolong or black tea made from this cultivar, use hotter water and follow the style rather than the plant.

vintage_note: Sencha from this cultivar is sold as the current year's spring harvest, as is usual for Japanese green tea. Oolong and black tea versions appear as small single-cultivar lots from Miyazaki growers, usually labelled with cultivar and maker.
description:
Minamisayaka is a Miyazaki cultivar that people seek out for its smell: milky, floral and fresh, and different enough from Yabukita that Japanese tea professionals disagree about whether they like it.

It was bred for sencha, where it gives a bright green leaf. Growers have since taken it further, into kamairicha, oolong and black tea, because that aroma carries well into other styles.

As a sencha, brew it cool and short like any other, and pay attention to the nose of the empty cup. The aromatic style is the point, so do not judge it only by how close it comes to a classic Yabukita.

It is a good cultivar to buy twice: once as sencha and once as a Takachiho or Gokase oolong or black tea, to see what the same plant does in different hands.

For growers it has real appeal as well, with higher yields than Yabukita and resistance to white peach scale, anthracnose and gray blight.
history: The cross, Miya A-6 × NN27, was made in 1970 at Miyazaki's agricultural research institute, and the seedlings were selected over about two decades. It was registered in 1991 as tea cultivar number 42. Kumamoto trials found it slightly later than Yabukita, productive at both first and second flush, and resistant to white peach scale.
